text: AI agents can propose a database change in seconds. But during an online migration, one bad ordering can silently corrupt the result. CutoverProof puts that ordering on trial before production.

The browser discovers five narrow WebMCP tools. It lists the bounded migration contracts, then inspects the status-normalization contract: declared phases, allowed operations, one invariant, and a hard authority boundary. No SQL has executed.
I ask CutoverProof to check stale legacy writes and compatibility-window ordering before cutover. The request is plain language, but the work stays inside the declared contract.

WebMCP creates an idempotent review draft, not an execution. The draft appears in the workspace as awaiting human review. An engineer can inspect the candidate budget, operations, invariant count, and isolated environment before anything runs.
Only the visible human control starts the assessment. CutoverProof resets its dedicated PostgreSQL sandbox, plans bounded schedules, executes them, and checks the invariant with deterministic code.

The verifier finds a real counterexample and blocks cutover. Backfill ran before a legacy update, leaving status shipped while the new lookup still says pending. The model suggested what to test; PostgreSQL decided what happened.
WebMCP reads the verifier-owned evidence: the exact failing schedule, the status-consistency invariant, and row forty-two. This is recorded from the test database, not generated by the model.

The agent may open the repair review, but it cannot approve. A named engineer authorizes one allow-listed sandbox fix. CutoverProof replays the same failing schedule, and the invariant now passes. The claim stays precise: repair verified in sandbox.
Agent prepares. PostgreSQL proves. Human authorizes.
